items.title: fix(ci): build the Espresso APK for x86_64 only
items.body:
The first combined nightly run ([29258504314](https://github.com/AKogut/mobile-task-manager-automation/actions/runs/29258504314)) executed **zero** Espresso tests. The app died during `MainApplication.onCreate`:

```
SoLoaderDSONotFoundError: couldn't find DSO to load: libreactnative.so
  Native lib dir: .../lib/arm64
  SoSource 1: DirectApkSoSource[root = base.apk!/lib/x86_64]
```

## Cause
Without `-PreactNativeArchitectures`, the APK carries every ABI. The API 35 `google_apis` image can translate arm64, so the package manager selected **arm64** as the app's primary ABI — and then looked for React Native's `.so` files in a directory that holds none. The crash happens at process start, which is why the suite reported no test results at all rather than failing tests.

## Fix
Pass `-PreactNativeArchitectures=x86_64`, exactly as the Appium Android job has always done:

```
# appium-suite.yml
./gradlew assembleRelease -PreactNativeArchitectures=x86_64
```

The evidence was already in the repository — the working Android job restricts the ABI, and the new Espresso job did not.

## Why local runs never caught this
The local emulator on an Apple Silicon machine is arm64, so the APK's arm64 libraries are the right ones and the app starts normally. The suite has been green locally throughout (49/49). This failure only exists on an x86_64 host, which is what CI is.

## What already worked
Everything else in the CI wiring did its job on that same run: KVM, the emulator, the SDK, the `TestIds.kt` drift check, artifact upload, and the aggregate step. The combined report published with **all four cards**, and `/android-native/` serves HTTP 200 — the Espresso card simply links a report of a run that crashed.

## Verification
The failure and the fix are both CI-only, so the honest verification is the next nightly run. I will dispatch it once this merges and confirm the Espresso job goes green with 49/49.

Documented in `android-tests/README.md` so the next person does not lose an hour to it.

items.title: fix: ref-complete history rewrites and persistent finding selection (0.6.0)
items.body:
Fixes three reported defects in the scan-results → cleanup flow.

## 1. No way to select findings

The results table rendered every checkbox hardcoded to `checked`, with no select-all / clear-all.

**Fix:** header master checkbox (with `indeterminate` for partial), `☑️ Select all` / `☐ Clear all` buttons, and a live *"N of M cleanable findings selected"* counter. Prepare buttons are disabled while nothing is selected.

## 2. Preparing a command re-checked every box

Selection and replacement text lived **only** in the webview DOM. `_prepareScanReplacementCommand()` calls `_updateWebviewContent()`, which does `webview.html = ...` — a full DOM rebuild. Every prepare reset the checkboxes to `checked` and the replacement inputs to `*****`, so unchecking a box was pointless.

**Fix:** selection (`Set<index>`) and replacement values move into `_scanCleanup` state and are rendered from there. The webview mirrors each change back via `scan.setSelection` / `scan.setAllSelection` / `scan.setReplacement`. `_resolveScanReplacements()` now reads persisted state rather than trusting the DOM payload.

## 3. The generated code did not enforce updates on all remote branches

Every rewrite path ended in `git push --force --all`, which expands to `refs/heads/*` **only**. A branch that existed solely as `refs/remotes/origin/*` was rewritten locally by `filter-branch -- --all` but never pushed — the leaked secret survived on the server and came back on the next fetch.

**Fix:** new `git-rewrite.js` implements the sequence from the reference implementation (`githistory.sh`), shared by all four rewrite call sites *and* by the generated script:

1. `git fetch --prune --tags origin`
2. **Block** if any local branch holds commits the remote lacks (step 4 would discard them)
3. Detach `HEAD` — git refuses to force-update the checked-out branch
4. **Materialise a local branch for every remote branch** ← the actual bug fix
5. Rewrite across all refs
6. Drop `refs/original/*`, expire reflog, `gc`
7. `git push --force --atomic --all` / `--tags`
8. Restore the originally checked-out branch
9. Re-fetch and **verify every remote branch and tag**

`--atomic` matters: without it a rejected ref (protected branch) leaves the remote half-rewritten — some branches clean, others still leaking.

The prepared output is now a complete, reviewable bash script (copy, or `💾 Save as .sh`) instead of an unreadable `&&` chain, plus a ref-by-ref **push plan** showing what will be force-updated / created.

## Also fixed while here

- **`git filter-repo` deletes the `origin` remote by design**, so the chained `&& git push --force --all` could never succeed. The URL is captured beforehand and the remote restored before pushing.
- **A failed BFG run fell through to the force-push stage**, rewriting the remote for a rewrite that never happened. Failures now abort before any push.
- **git-history keyword findings rendered as selectable** but were silently dropped at resolve time (the row renderer and the resolver disagreed). One `_isCleanupEligible()` predicate now covers both.

Closes LL-001 (mandatory full ref refresh before rewrite) and LL-002 (explicit ref-aware push plan).

## Verification

**Unit tests** — `npm test`, 18 passing (was 4). New suites cover script generation (materialisation loop present, every push `--atomic`, verify-after-push ordering, remote restoration) and selection state (eligibility, deselection surviving a re-render, clear/select-all round-trip, per-finding replacement values, reset on rescan).

**End-to-end, against a real bare remote.** Fixture: a repo whose `remote-only` branch exists solely as `refs/remotes/origin/*` locally, plus a tag.

Old behaviour (`git push --force --all`):
```
refs/heads/main:        .github/workflows/ci.yml README.md
refs/heads/remote-only: .github/workflows/ci.yml README.md other-secret.txt secret.txt   <== LEAK
```

New behaviour, both via the extension runner and by executing the generated script:
```
refs/heads/main:        .github/workflows/ci.yml README.md
refs/heads/remote-only: .github/workflows/ci.yml README.md
refs/tags/v1.0.0:       .github/workflows/ci.yml README.md
server history: no commit introduces SUPERSECRETVALUE123
restored branch: main
Verified clean on every remote ref.
```

**Preflight block** — with an unpushed local commit, both the script and `runRewrite()` refuse (`AheadBranchesError: ... main (+1)`) and the remote is left untouched.

`npm run lint`: 0 errors, warning count unchanged from `main`.

Note: `npm run lint` also walks `node_modules` (pre-existing gap in `eslint.config.mjs`, only visible once deps are installed) — left alone as out of scope.

items.title: Add CLAUDE.md and REVIEW.md

labels.name: documentation
labels.description: Improvements or additions to documentation: instructions, concepts, analyses

items.body:
## What

Two guidance files, plus the one-line CI consistency fix that writing them uncovered.

**`CLAUDE.md`** — what an agent needs before touching anything: the supported version ranges and the fact that CI derives the PHP floor from the Nextcloud `min-version`, the layout, the commands, the four places a version lives, and the conventions (SPDX/REUSE, SHA-pinned actions, `.nextcloudignore` decisions, translatable texts, terse changelog lines, when to parametrise a test, SOLID pragmatically). It closes with the three things that look like mistakes and are deliberate.

**`REVIEW.md`** — what review should pay attention to in an app that guards a login: missing brute-force, password-confirmation or admin-authorisation attributes, code handling and lifetime, empty results reported as success, failure paths that cannot work, shell portability in dev tooling. And, just as important, a list of what is **already decided**, so the same pins and trade-offs are not re-litigated every time.

## Reviewed before pushing

I ran `/code-review` on the first draft. It produced eight findings and every one of them was real; each was verified against the code before I acted on it.

Two were false statements: "root-level Markdown is covered by `REUSE.toml`" (it is an explicit filename list — which is why these two files had to be added by hand), and a wrong description of `templates/` (four files, one of which is the enrolment step shown during login, not a settings page).

Three would have produced a finding in **every** future review — the opposite of the point:

| Would have been flagged forever | Why it is correct as it is |
|---|---|
| `resend()` without `#[PasswordConfirmationRequired]` | it runs before the second factor, where confirmation cannot be satisfied; rate limit, brute-force protection and cooldown guard it |
| a wrong code not invalidating the stored one | deliberate: users may mistype |
| `curl` without `-f` in `tests/smoke/` | the status code *is* the assertion there |

One made a pin look permanent: the `@nextcloud/vite-config` pre-release expires as soon as a stable release supports Vite 8, and stating it without that condition silences the rule meant to catch it.

The last two: both files **shipped inside the release package** (`.nextcloudignore` lists filenames and had no entry for them — verified fixed: the built package now contains zero matches while `README`/`SECURITY`/`CONTRIBUTORS`/`CHANGELOG` still ship), and `CLAUDE.md` never mentioned `REVIEW.md`, so an agent reading the file it is guaranteed to load never learned the review guidance existed.

## The CI commit

`test.yml`'s second checkout was the only one of twelve without `persist-credentials: false`. It surfaced while writing the convention down: a rule the repository itself breaks in one place is not a rule yet. Separate commit, one line.

## Base

Stacked on #165 because both files link to `doc/releasing.md` and `tests/smoke/README.md`. GitHub retargets this to `main` once #165 is merged.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code), verified, tweaked and approved by @nursoda.
